findings.source_passage: He was still bewildered by the introduction of tragedy into his cheerful commonplace existence.
findings.source_locator: After 'Back at the Ritz, Tommy packed up his few belongings mechanically'
findings.why_it_matters: The source phrase 'his cheerful commonplace existence' is a deliberately ironic voice marker — Christie's narrator uses 'existence' (not 'life') to underline the bathos of adventure intruding on ordinariness; the draft substitutes 'cheerful commonplace life,' losing the precise diction.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'cheerful commonplace existence' verbatim rather than 'cheerful commonplace life.'

findings.source_passage: That functionary, however, merely replied respectfully: 'Yes, sir. Shall I call a taxi?'
findings.source_locator: After Tommy says 'I'm going to the devil'
findings.why_it_matters: Christie's identification of the servant as 'That functionary' is a light satirical register marker — the narrator's ironic distance from the scene. The draft omits the label entirely, cutting the voice beat that provides dry comic relief at an emotionally heavy moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'That functionary, however, merely replied respectfully' before the taxi line.

findings.source_passage: 'You were up against one of the biggest brains of the century. And you came very near success. Remember that.'
findings.source_locator: Mr. Carter's consolation speech to Tommy, after 'Don't take it to heart, lad'
findings.why_it_matters: Mr. Carter's characterisation of Mr. Brown as 'one of the biggest brains of the century' carries interpretive weight — it is the novel's clearest authorial testimony to the villain's stature, and Tommy's near-success is the only mitigation he is offered. The draft omits this entirely, losing both the villain-framing and the emotional beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Carter's full consolation: 'Don't take it to heart, lad… You were up against one of the biggest brains of the century. And you came very near success. Remember that.'

findings.source_passage: "I've been the most almighty blithering darned idiot that it's possible to imagine."
findings.source_locator: Julius's speech after anger drops, before 'Calm down'
findings.why_it_matters: The full self-deprecating phrase 'the most almighty blithering darned idiot that it's possible to imagine' is a stylistically distinctive piece of Julius's transatlantic voice — its extravagance is the point. The draft trims to 'the most almighty blithering idiot,' losing 'darned' and 'that it's possible to imagine,' which deflates the comic/self-aware register.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'I've been the most almighty blithering darned idiot that it's possible to imagine.'

findings.source_passage: He came to himself with a start. 'I'm taking up your time, sir,' he said with an effort.
findings.why_it_matters: The stage direction 'Tommy came to himself with a start' signals the precise moment Tommy regathers self-control after his outburst; the draft drops it and moves straight to the dialogue, softening the psychological specificity Christie gives to the scene.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Tommy came to himself with a start' before 'I'm taking up your time, sir.'

summary: Three medium-severity findings — the erasure of Carter's 'biggest brains of the century' consolation (interpretive weight on the villain), the truncation of Julius's self-deprecating speech (voice register), and the loss of Carter's 'Don't take it to heart, lad' beat — collectively trigger a regenerate verdict.
